summaries.example: Imagine saying “the tallest student is carrying a book.” Instead of treating “the tallest student” as a mysterious object, we can explain the whole sentence: there is exactly one student taller than everyone else, and that student is carrying a book. The phrase gets its meaning from how it works in a sentence.
summaries.summary: Logical construction is Russell’s name for several projects that use definitions and logic to replace guesses about special objects. For example, the number two can be described as the class of all groups with two members. Russell also explained definite descriptions, such as “the tallest student,” by showing how a complete sentence says that one and only one person has the relevant feature. Classes, numbers, ordered series, functions, and even parts of the physical world were studied in related ways. The goal was often to prove useful facts from definitions rather than merely assume them. The entry stresses that these projects are not all identical. Some treat expressions as incomplete symbols, while others are reductions or mathematical reconstructions. Philosophers later debated whether logical construction formed one unified method and used it in work on science, language, and mathematics.
key_ideas: Bertrand Russell used logic to rebuild ideas instead of simply assuming that hidden objects existed.
He defined numbers through groups of groups that have the same number of members.
Some expressions, such as “the tallest student,” are best explained by rewriting the whole sentence.
Russell and Alfred North Whitehead also explored how space, time, matter, and mathematics might be described using simpler elements.
Logical construction is not always exactly the same method; different examples share a family resemblance.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logical construction teaches an important habit of careful thinking: before assuming that something mysterious exists, ask whether its useful features can be explained using simpler ideas. This approach influenced logical analysis, theories of science, and later ways of making unclear ideas more precise. It also shows that explaining an idea may involve changing how a sentence works, not just giving a short dictionary definition.

important_terms.definition: A method of explaining something by defining it from things we already understand, then using logic to show what follows.
A phrase that does not stand for a complete thing by itself; its meaning appears when it is used in a whole sentence.
A group of things treated together, such as all pairs of objects.
A phrase that picks out one particular thing by saying what kind of thing it is and that there is only one.

questions_to_think_about: When is it better to explain an idea from familiar parts instead of assuming it is basic?
Does a phrase need to name a thing in order to be useful?
Can two different definitions help us understand the same idea?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, when we replace an everyday idea with a logical description?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “the average family has 2.2 children.” Russell’s approach does not require an object called the average family. Instead, the statement can be rewritten as a claim about the total number of children divided by the number of families. “The average family” is therefore meaningful in context even though no single family is the average family. This illustrates contextual definition and the distinction between surface grammar and logical form.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines a group of projects Bertrand Russell later called logical constructions. Their common thread is methodological rather than a single uniform definition: a theory begins with relatively basic notions and introduces definitions from which “neat” properties of more complex or apparently theoretical entities can be derived. This contrasts with simply postulating entities that satisfy axioms. Russell’s definition of natural numbers as classes of equinumerous classes is a model case. The theory of definite descriptions is different in form: a description is handled through contextual definition, so a sentence containing “the F” is rewritten using quantifiers and identity. Class expressions receive a related treatment in the no-classes theory, while series, ordinal numbers, and real numbers are more naturally viewed as mathematical constructions whose properties become theorems. Descriptive functions are analyzed as definite descriptions based on relations. The status of propositions and propositional functions is less settled, since their supposed contextual definitions are not fully supplied and their ontological interpretation remains debated. Russell’s later construction of matter, space, and time from sense data or sensibilia extends the project toward physics, but it makes the comparison among the different constructions especially difficult. Later philosophers connected the approach with analysis, scientific reconstruction, Carnap’s Aufbau, Quine’s explication, measurement theory, and structural realism. The entry therefore presents logical construction as a connected family of methods rather than an entirely uniform procedure.
key_ideas: Russell’s constructions were designed to derive formerly postulated properties from definitions and logical principles. The natural numbers provide the clearest example: a number is defined as a class of classes that can be put into one-to-one correspondence.

Logical analysis and logical construction are not simply opposite operations. Analysis concerns the structure or constituents of propositions, while construction develops a formal theory in which selected statements can be proved.

The theory of definite descriptions uses contextual definition: “The F is G” is treated as saying that exactly one thing is F and that it is G. This helps explain how descriptions can function without naming independent objects.

Russell’s treatment of classes similarly avoids taking class expressions as ordinary singular terms, but the entry cautions that this is a reduction to propositional functions, not necessarily a claim that classes are mere make-believe.
The treatment of series, ordinals, real numbers, and mathematical functions shows that construction can be a precise mathematical definition, not just an attempt to remove questionable entities.
Russell’s construction of matter, space, and time from sense data or sensibilia raises a harder question: how can a method suited to numbers or descriptions apply to the physical world?
summaries.why_it_matters: Logical construction helped shape analytic philosophy’s interest in logical form, formal definitions, and the relation between language and ontology. It offers a way to replace doubtful inferences with deductions from specified starting points, while also revealing that different constructions serve different purposes: elimination, reduction, mathematical definition, or scientific reconstruction. The later disputes matter because they test whether formal success is enough, whether ordinary meaning can be preserved, and whether structures derived from experience tell us about the world itself.

important_terms.definition: A Russellian strategy of defining or reconstructing entities so that important properties follow logically from more basic notions rather than being introduced as unexplained assumptions.
A definition that explains an expression by providing rules for rewriting complete sentences containing it, rather than by assigning it an isolated object or term.
An expression whose meaning is supplied by its role in a larger proposition; it need not have a complete meaning in isolation.
An entity or expression treated as eliminable or reducible through logical analysis, though the entry warns that “fiction” does not fit every construction equally well.
A relation in which members can be paired one-to-one; Russell used this notion to define numbers as classes of equally numerous classes.
A sentence-like expression with one or more open places, such as “x is human,” which can produce propositions when arguments are supplied.
Potential objects of sensation in Russell’s account; perceived sensibilia become sense data for a perceiver.
A methodological project that gives a precise substitute for a less precise or incomplete ordinary notion, sometimes by choosing among several acceptable definitions.

questions_to_think_about: Should a successful theory be judged mainly by what it can prove, or must it also preserve every feature of ordinary language and experience?
Does rewriting a sentence eliminate an object, or can it merely show that the object is not fundamental to the theory?
Why might a contextual definition be preferable to an explicit definition of a single term?
If several constructions satisfy the same formal requirement, does choosing among them reveal a fact or make a useful convention?
Can the construction of physical objects from experiences explain their reality, or does it leave an important gap?

summaries.example: Suppose a class has four students and another class has four books. We can pair each student with one book, with none left over. Russell would call the two classes similar or equinumerous. His idea was that the number four can be understood as the class of all classes that can be paired one-to-one with any four-member class. The number is not introduced only by listing its usual properties; it is built through a definition.
summaries.summary: “Logical construction” is a name Russell gave, especially in retrospect, to several related projects in logic, mathematics, language, and philosophy of science. The basic strategy is to begin with selected notions and definitions, then derive properties that might otherwise have been accepted only as axioms or assumptions. His definition of natural numbers illustrates the strategy: the number two is the class of all classes whose members can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the members of any pair. Russell’s theory of definite descriptions uses a different technique. A sentence such as “the F is G” is understood as saying that there is exactly one F and that it is G. The description is not treated as a separate name for an object; its role is explained within the complete sentence. The no-classes theory uses a similar contextual approach. Other examples include series and ordinal numbers, real numbers built from earlier number systems, and mathematical functions treated through descriptions based on relations. Russell also discussed propositions and propositional functions, although their precise status and the possibility of giving them contextual definitions are disputed. His later work with Whitehead’s ideas about constructing matter, space, and time from sense data or sensibilia made the method relevant to physics but also exposed its limits. Later thinkers developed related approaches in scientific reconstruction, measurement theory, and Quine’s explication.
key_ideas: Russell preferred carefully proving mathematical facts from definitions and logic rather than simply assuming axioms describe some existing objects.
The natural-number construction defines a number through all classes with the same size, using one-to-one matching.
The analysis of definite descriptions separates ordinary grammar from logical form. “The F is G” becomes a claim that exactly one thing is F and that it is G.
Not every construction has the same status. Some are incomplete symbols, some are called logical fictions, and others are ordinary mathematical definitions or reductions.
Russell and Whitehead extended related ideas to functions, orderings, ordinal numbers, real numbers, propositions, and the physical world.
Philosophers disagreed about whether these examples form one unified method and about whether constructions really remove commitment to the things they discuss.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logical constructions connect abstract logic with ordinary questions about what exists and how language works. They show how a philosopher might reduce a complicated idea, make an unclear expression precise, or replace an unsupported assumption with a formal derivation. The approach also teaches caution: a method that works cleanly for numbers may not work in exactly the same way for tables, physical objects, or experiences.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical method that defines or reconstructs an apparently higher-level idea from simpler notions so that its important properties can be proved.
A way to define an expression by explaining how entire sentences containing it should be rewritten.
A symbol or phrase whose meaning depends on its use inside a complete sentence rather than on standing for an object by itself.
Two classes are equinumerous when their members can be matched one-to-one, with each member of one class matched to exactly one member of the other.
A sentence pattern with an open place, such as “x is taller than y,” that becomes a proposition when suitable terms replace the variables.
A mathematical relation that is transitive, connected, and irreflexive; such relations provide orderings or series.
Possible objects of sensation; when a person actually experiences them, they function as sense data for that person.

questions_to_think_about: Why might proving the properties of numbers be better than merely starting with axioms about numbers?
What happens to the meaning of “the F” when there is no unique F?
Is a class a real object, a useful way of speaking, or something reducible to properties and logic?
Why is constructing matter from sense data more philosophically difficult than defining a number?
Can a precise replacement for an everyday idea still count as an explanation of that idea?
